description: Daily energy needs, macronutrients, balanced diet ratios and the effects of dehydration on sport.
content_html:
Energy: The Fuel for Sport and Life

Everything the body does — breathing, thinking, sprinting, lifting — requires energy. That energy is measured in kilocalories (Kcal) and comes entirely from the food we eat. The average adult male requires approximately 2,500 Kcal per day, while the average adult female requires around 2,000 Kcal per day. However, these are only averages — how much energy any individual actually needs depends on four key factors: age, gender, height, and energy expenditure (how much exercise they do). A 16-year-old county-level swimmer training twice a day will have far greater energy needs than a sedentary adult of the same height and gender.

Key Fact

An individual’s daily energy requirement is affected by age, gender, height, and energy expenditure. Average values are 2,500 Kcal/day for males and 2,000 Kcal/day for females — but athletes and highly active individuals need significantly more.

The Balanced Diet: Proportions and Purposes

A balanced diet does not mean eating equal amounts of everything. It means eating the right proportions of different food types to supply the body with all the nutrients it needs. No single food provides every nutrient — variety is essential. Unused energy, particularly from saturated fats, is stored as body fat, which can contribute to obesity over time. The specification requires you to know the approximate percentage breakdown of a balanced diet: 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, and 15–20% protein. These proportions reflect the primary roles each macronutrient plays in the body.

Macronutrients: Carbohydrate, Fat and Protein

Carbohydrate is the primary and preferred fuel for all types of exercise, regardless of intensity. Whether a performer is jogging at a comfortable pace or sprinting at maximum effort, carbohydrates are the first fuel the body calls upon. They are broken down into glucose, which is either used immediately or stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver for use during exercise. Elite distance runners such as Dina Asher-Smith prepare for competition partly by ensuring glycogen stores are fully loaded through carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before an event.

Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate, but it can only be used efficiently as a fuel source at low intensity — for example, during a slow, steady-state walk or easy cycle ride. When exercise intensity increases, the body switches back to carbohydrate because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the demand. Fat also has important non-energy roles: it insulates the body, protects organs, and is a carrier for fat-soluble vitamins.

Protein is not a primary energy source. Its main role is the growth and repair of muscle tissue — essential after heavy training when muscle fibres have been broken down by the work they have done. Adam Peaty, for example, follows a protein-rich recovery plan after intense pool sessions to support muscle repair and adaptation. Consuming insufficient protein slows recovery and limits the adaptations (such as hypertrophy) that training is designed to produce.

Vitamins and minerals do not supply energy directly, but they are essential for the efficient working of all body systems. Vitamins support processes from immune function to bone health; minerals such as calcium and iron are vital for bone density and oxygen transport in the blood respectively. The specification does not require you to name specific vitamins or minerals, but you should know that their role is to maintain the efficient working of body systems and general health. A diet lacking in variety will typically be deficient in vitamins and minerals even if its Kcal total looks adequate on paper.

Key Fact

A balanced diet is approximately 55–60% carbohydrate (main energy source), 25–30% fat (energy at low intensity; insulation), 15–20% protein (growth and repair). Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities.

Hydration and the Consequences of Dehydration

Water is not just a drink — it is the medium in which almost every chemical reaction in the body takes place. Maintaining water balance (hydration) is critical to performance. Even a 1–2% reduction in body mass through fluid loss can begin to impair sporting performance. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. During intense exercise in warm conditions — such as a cross-country race or a summer football tournament — sweat rates can be high, meaning fluid must be replaced regularly to maintain performance and safety.

Effects of Dehydration on the Body and Performance

Dehydration triggers a series of interconnected physiological problems. As fluid is lost, blood plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker. This increase in blood viscosity means the heart must work harder to push blood around the circulatory system, driving up heart rate. Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles slows, accelerating fatigue. In severe cases, heart rhythm may become irregular. Meanwhile, the body’s ability to shed heat through the blood vessels near the skin is compromised, causing core body temperature to rise — increasing the risk of overheating and heat stroke.

Beyond the cardiovascular effects, dehydration also affects the nervous system. Reaction time slows and decision-making deteriorates — a basketball player who is even mildly dehydrated may make slower, poorer decisions on court. Muscle function degrades too: dehydrated muscles fatigue more rapidly and are more prone to cramping, because the electrolyte balance (sodium, potassium) that enables muscle contraction is disrupted. For a sprint cyclist like Geraint Thomas, any cramping or slowing of reaction time in the final kilometre of a race could be decisive.

A common misconception is that hydration simply means “drink lots.” The spec focuses on balance — maintaining appropriate water levels, not overloading with fluids. The assessment reward is for understanding the cascade of effects from dehydration: thicker blood → higher heart rate → slower delivery of oxygen → muscle fatigue/cramp → slower reactions → poorer decisions. Practise writing that chain in order without notes, anchored to a sporting example.
exam_tip_html:
On “Calculate” and “Calculate from Data” questions involving nutrition, always show your working, state the units (Kcal, %, g) and box your final answer. If asked to calculate the energy from carbohydrate in a diet of 2,400 Kcal, the working is: 2,400 × 0.55 = 1,320 Kcal from carbohydrate (or 2,400 × 0.60 = 1,440 Kcal at the upper end of the range). Missing the unit drops a mark.

On a 6-mark “Analyse” question about dehydration, avoid listing effects without connecting them. Write each effect as a cause-and-effect chain: “Dehydration reduces blood plasma volume, which increases blood viscosity (thickness). The heart must then beat faster to maintain blood flow, leading to earlier fatigue, and reduced oxygen delivery to working muscles.” That single chain earns more credit than five disconnected bullet points.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is measured in Kcal. Daily needs (avg. 2,500 Kcal male / 2,000 Kcal female) vary with age, gender, height and exercise levels. A balanced diet is 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, 15–20% protein — carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all intensities.
  • Protein’s role is growth and repair of muscle tissue. Fat provides energy only at low intensity and in larger amounts than carbohydrate per gram. Vitamins and minerals maintain efficient body system function.
  • Dehydration increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate, causes overheating, slows reactions, impairs decision-making and causes muscle fatigue and cramps — all of which degrade sporting performance.

practice_questions.text: Identify the macronutrient that the body uses as its main and preferred energy source for all types of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: carbohydrate (accept carbs / glucose / glycogen — the macronutrient name is the target).

practice_questions.text: A sports nutritionist tells a 16-year-old female athlete that her daily diet provides 2,200 Kcal. Calculate the minimum and maximum amount of energy (in Kcal) that should come from carbohydrate in her balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: Formula: Kcal from carbohydrate = total Kcal × percentage. Minimum: 2,200 × 0.55 = 1,210 Kcal (1 mark). Maximum: 2,200 × 0.60 = 1,320 Kcal (1 mark). Both values required for full marks; unit (Kcal) must be stated or implied by context.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the daily food intake of two junior rugby players during a pre-season training week.

Player | Total daily Kcal | % from carbohydrate | % from protein | % from fat
Jamie  | 3,100 Kcal       | 50%                 | 20%            | 30%
Tyler  | 3,100 Kcal       | 58%                 | 17%            | 25%

Using the data, calculate the number of Kcal that Tyler obtains from carbohydrate each day, and state whether his carbohydrate intake falls within the recommended range for a balanced diet.
practice_questions.marks: Working: 3,100 × 0.58 = 1,798 Kcal from carbohydrate (1 mark for correct working). Final answer: 1,798 Kcal (1 mark). Balanced diet range is 55–60%, so 58% falls within the recommended range (1 mark for correct judgement with reference to the 55–60% figure). Unit (Kcal) must be present.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the resting and exercising heart rates of two athletes before and after a 90-minute training session in hot conditions. Athlete A drank water throughout; Athlete B drank nothing.

Athlete | Heart rate before session (bpm) | Heart rate at 75 min (bpm)
A       | 68                              | 142
B       | 70                              | 167

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of dehydration on Athlete B's heart rate, and explain why this change occurred.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Athlete B's heart rate is higher than Athlete A's at 75 minutes (167 bpm vs 142 bpm — a difference of 25 bpm). 1 mark for a comparison that quotes both figures. 1 mark for linking the higher heart rate to dehydration causing increased blood viscosity (thicker blood). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the heart must beat faster/work harder to maintain blood flow to muscles when blood is thicker. Quoting figures without making a comparison earns 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A club-level triathlete has been advised by her coach to increase her protein intake during a 10-week strength-building phase. Analyse how an appropriate increase in protein, alongside sufficient carbohydrate, would support her training adaptations over this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained analysis linking protein's role in muscle repair and hypertrophy to strength adaptations; explains that protein alone is insufficient without carbohydrate to fuel training sessions (carbohydrate = preferred energy source, all intensities); applies correctly to the triathlete context (heavy training, strength-building); may reference recovery between sessions; accurate use of terms (hypertrophy, glycogen, muscle fibre repair). Secure (3–4 marks): Accurate points about protein's role in repair/growth and carbohydrate as fuel; at least one point linked to the athlete's context; some development of each point. Developing (2 marks): Correct function of protein stated (growth and repair); carbohydrate mentioned; limited development or application to sport. Emerging (1 mark): One basic accurate point about protein or carbohydrate in isolation, with little or no sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A Year-11 PE class has been asked whether the government should make sports drinks mandatory for school athletes during competition. Evaluate whether sports drinks are necessary to maintain hydration and performance during school-level sport, considering the consequences of dehydration.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced, sustained evaluation with both sides argued; consequences of dehydration cited accurately (increased blood viscosity, raised heart rate, slowed reactions, muscle cramps, impaired decision-making); counter-argument addresses the reality that most school-level sport is short-duration and water is sufficient; may distinguish between low-intensity school sport and high-intensity endurance events; correct use of terminology throughout; sporting examples used to anchor both sides. Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides present; dehydration consequences mostly accurate; sporting application present; some terminology. Developing (3–4 marks): One side argued well; dehydration mentioned but effects may be listed without development; limited balance. Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about hydration being important with little or no balance or application.

knowledge_checks.q: What percentage of a balanced diet should come from carbohydrate?
Which effect does dehydration have on the blood?
options: It makes blood thinner and faster-flowing
It increases blood viscosity, slowing blood flow
It reduces the number of red blood cells
It lowers heart rate by reducing blood pressure

knowledge_checks.q: Fat can only be used efficiently as a fuel during _____ intensity exercise.
The role of protein in sport is primarily the growth and _____ of muscle tissue.
Match each macronutrient to its primary role:
right: Main energy source for exercise at all intensities
Growth and repair of muscle tissue
Energy source at low intensity; insulation and organ protection

flashcard_questions.q: What is the average daily energy requirement for an adult male?
What is the average daily energy requirement for an adult female?
How does exercise level affect an individual's daily energy requirement?
flashcard_questions.a: Greater energy expenditure through exercise increases the total Kcal needed each day.

flashcard_questions.q: What percentage of a balanced diet should come from carbohydrate?
What percentage of a balanced diet should come from protein?
At what exercise intensity can fat be used efficiently as a fuel source?
What is the primary role of protein in sport and exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Growth and repair of muscle tissue.
A state where fluid lost by the body exceeds fluid taken in.

flashcard_questions.q: How does dehydration affect blood viscosity?
flashcard_questions.a: It increases viscosity — blood becomes thicker and flows more slowly.

flashcard_questions.q: Dehydration increases blood viscosity. What happens to heart rate as a result?
flashcard_questions.a: Heart rate increases as the heart works harder to pump thicker blood.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two effects of dehydration on muscle function.
How does dehydration affect body temperature during exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: Core temperature rises, increasing the risk of overheating.

flashcard_questions.q: What role do vitamins and minerals play in a balanced diet?
flashcard_questions.a: Maintaining efficient working of body systems and general health.

glossary_terms.definition: A unit of energy used in nutrition; food energy is measured in kilocalories where 1 Kcal equals 1,000 calories.
A diet that contains the correct proportions of all essential nutrients the body needs for health, growth and energy.
The body's main and preferred energy source for exercise, broken down into glucose and stored as glycogen in muscle and liver.
A macronutrient used primarily for the growth and repair of muscle tissue, not as a major energy source during exercise.
A state of insufficient water in the body, caused when fluid lost through sweat, respiration and urine exceeds fluid taken in.
The thickness or resistance to flow of blood; dehydration increases blood viscosity, making it harder for the heart to pump blood to working muscles.
